newsitem.title: USA: U.S. worried by rapid rise in Japanese car imports.
newsitem.headline: U.S. worried by rapid rise in Japanese car imports.

text.p: U.S. trade officials expressed concern on Friday about rising Japanese car imports into the U.S. market and said Tokyo needed to do more to open Japan's markets to U.S. car products.
In an assessment of a hard-fought 1995 car trade agreement between the two countries, U.S. trade officials said progress has generally been positive.
But they expressed disappointment in the pace of deregulation of Japan's car parts markets and in the low number of dealerships that have agreed to sell U.S.-made cars in Japan.

"We are pleased that progress continues to be made under the agreement," U.S. Secretary of Commerce William Daley said in a statement. "U.S. vehicle sales in Japan jumped 34 percent and exports of U.S.-made automotive parts rose to $2 billion in 1996, an increase of 20 percent over 1995."

The 1995 agreement aimed at opening Japan's market to more U.S.-made cars and parts was reached only after intense negotiations during which the two countries were on the brink of a tit-for-tat trade war.

U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said that despite market access gains last year, she was concerned about developing trade trends. She cited concerns about rising Japanese car imports in the U.S. market during the first three months of the year.

"We don't want to see a significant increase in the Japanese trade surplus," Barshefsky said. "The overall imbalance in U.S.-Japan auto trade and the first quarter surge in Japanese imports requires that we watch this situation closely."
The report, which was sent to President Bill Clinton, said that a weakening yen against the dollar has benefited Japanese car makers at the expense of U.S. firms.

Despite early gains after the 1995 agreement was signed, sales in Japan by the Big Three U.S. automakers -- Chrysler Corp., Ford Motor Co. and General Motors Corp. -- began to level off during later 1996 and declined in the first three months of 1997.

"In contrast, sales of European-made vehicles (including those produced by the Big Three) to Japan began to grow faster, in part because the yen did not depreciate as much against these currencies," the report said.

U.S. car makers have complained for months that the weakening yen against the dollar was hurting their sales to Japan and giving Japanese car makers a competitive edge in U.S. markets. A weak yen makes Japanese cars less expensive in the United States and U.S.-made cars more expensive in Japan.

The Big three chief executives met Wednesday with Vice President Al Gore to discuss the trade situation and other issues of concern to the automakers, industry officials said. The executives are also trying to arrange a meeting with Clinton to discuss their concerns about the yen.
Clinton and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto are scheduled to meet next Friday in Washington. U.S. officials have said trade concerns will be on the agenda.
The report said that imports of Japanese vehicles into the U.S. market began to increase in late 1996. In early 1997, Japanese car makers were starting grab a bigger share of the U.S. market.
It said Japanese dealers had been reluctant to agree to sell U.S.-made cars and only 114 new dealer outlets had been added by the Big Three U.S. automakers since the car trade agreement was signed.
The report also said more deregulation was needed in Japan's parts markets to provide opportunities for U.S. parts manufacturers.
